topics.topic: Allocation, ordering, uniqueness, and reuse of global record positions
questions: How is the single durable store position assigned to every record, including multiple records written by one transaction, and can positions ever be reused after restore or cleanup?
What exactly is the global store order, when is a position allocated, and how are multiple records written by one transaction ordered?
Does every newly created durable record receive a unique global position, what is the order of multiple creations in one transaction, and does updating a record preserve or change its position?

judgement.why: The topic repeats the previously judged question about global positions, updates and multi-record transaction ordering.

precedent.topic: Store-position assignment and ordering within one transaction
quotes: record_change: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] Every record written gets one store position from a single strictly increasing counter shared by all record types, assigned inside the transaction that writes it; store order is the order of these positions, every collection the module returns is in store order unless the function says otherwise, and Activation and FlowActivation records are identified by their store_position.

record_change: [BEHAVIOR] MUST apply the one StoreChange given in one SQLite transaction that either writes every record the variant lists or nothing; it writes no record the variant does not list and trusts the caller for every decision of the caller's rule, checking only its own invariants: attempt numbers, unique and existing identities, existing linked records, and no edit of an immutable record. Records of the kinds that are never edited — issued contract versions, implementations, trial cases, flow versions, values, verdicts, activations and trace records — are only ever written once; for any other entity a lifecycle change — a status, who decided, resolved, revoked, cancelled or released and when, concluded_at, ended_at, waiting points, outputs — updates those fields of the entity's one record in place, and the record keeps its store position, the position of its creation; no other field of a written record ever changes.

record_change: [FIELD_ASSIGNMENT] RecordRunProgressChange writes the NodeExecutions from its drafts with their StoredValues and SpooledFiles, then sets the run's status, outputs, waiting points (replacing the previous ones), ended_at and, when the new status is cancelled, cancelled_by; RecordResumptionChange appends one Resumption to the run; ReleaseRunChange sets released_by and released_at of the run.

record_change: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] attempt_number of a NodeExecution written by RecordRunProgressChange, RecordReadOutcomeChange, RecordOperationFailureChange or DecideApprovalChange, and of an EffectAttempt written by RecordAttemptInFlightChange, is one more than the number of NodeExecutions the element already has, and RequestApprovalChange gives the EffectApproval it writes that same next number as its attempt_number without writing a NodeExecution; RecordRunProgressChange writes its executions in (node_id, map_index) order with an absent map_index before index 0.
precedent.why: The texts define a global counter, preserve positions on updates, and order NodeExecution drafts, but do not give a complete position-assignment order for all new records written together by each StoreChange.

topics.topic: Atomic store-call and transaction boundaries across writes
questions: Does “every change” include filesystem-only publication, replacement and cleanup, and must each such action open a SQLite transaction?
Which filesystem actions belong to the atomic store call, when is the database committed, and when does a cleanup failure make the call fail versus leave the committed record standing?
For each multi-record action, which writes must commit atomically and which may remain committed if a later write in the same surface request fails or the process crashes?

quotes:
Each is one transaction (K-17); the module named is its only caller. Records
not listed are never written.

record_change: [BEHAVIOR] MUST apply the one StoreChange given in one SQLite transaction that either writes every record the variant lists or nothing; it writes no record the variant does not list and trusts the caller for every decision of the caller's rule, checking only its own invariants: attempt numbers, unique and existing identities, existing linked records, and no edit of an immutable record.

spool_file: [RETURN_SHAPE] Returns FileFacts with the hexadecimal SHA-256 content_digest, size_bytes and the given media_type; it writes no SpooledFile record, which the caller's later record_change writes.

remove_run_spool: [BEHAVIOR] MUST remove the spool directory of run_id and everything in it without following symbolic links, and return normally when the spool is already absent or the run is unknown; it never removes anything outside that one run's spool and writes no record.
remove_run_spool: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise StoreInternalError on an I/O failure while removing; callers treat that as a spool left for the next start, not as a failed request.
judgement.why: The later contracts enumerate each atomic record change and distinguish file publication and post-commit spool removal as separate filesystem-only calls.

topics.topic: Database initialization, migration, corruption, and compatibility rules
questions: What exact database conditions stop startup, and may the kernel ever initialize or migrate an existing database automatically?
When may the schema be initialized or migrated, and what startup result applies to corruption and unsupported schema versions?
Which database states initialize a new store, which are migrated, and which refuse startup without modifying existing data?

judgement.why: Database schemas, schema compatibility and migration policy belong to State 6 or later.

topics.topic: Event defining concurrent request serialization order
questions: What observable event assigns a request its place in the serial queue, and how are simultaneous arrivals ordered?
What event establishes the total order of concurrently arriving requests?
What event establishes the total arrival order, and are later concurrent requests queued or refused while one request is running?

judgement.why: The topic repeats the prior judgement about the event establishing total arrival order for concurrent surface requests.

precedent.topic: Definition of total arrival order for concurrent surface requests
quotes: serve_kernel: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] Requests are handled strictly one at a time, each to its end, run advancement included, before the next one is read (A18 rule 3).
precedent.why: The later surface contract establishes the total order by reading no next request until the current request has completed.

topics.topic: First-start data-directory layout and automatic creation
questions: Which missing-store states represent a new installation, and which cause startup refusal?
What are the exact paths, and which missing store objects are created on first start versus treated as store damage?
What must already exist on first start, and what storage structures may the kernel create automatically?

judgement.why: The topic repeats the prior judgement about creation of the data directory and missing internal store objects.

precedent.topic: Startup handling and creation of a missing data directory and required store objects
quotes: open_store: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise RefusedError whose reason names the failed check: data_directory does not exist (it is never created here), lock held by another process, directory not private (naming the first offending path), or symbolic link found (naming its path); it removes and creates nothing when a check fails.

The kernel never
creates the data directory itself: the owner creates it, private to the
kernel's user; inside it `open_store` creates the database schema, the
content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.
precedent.why: The later store API refuses a missing data directory but creates the database schema, content-addressed area, and spool area inside an existing valid directory.

topics.topic: Required ownership, permissions, and filesystem-object safety properties
questions: What exact ownership and permission predicates define “private” for the directory, subdirectories, database, SQLite sidecars, lock, temporary files, values, fixtures and spool files?
What ownership, file types, and permission bits must the root directory, subdirectories, database files, SQLite sidecars, blobs, fixtures, spool files, lock file, and temporary files have?
Which ownership, permission, file-type, hard-link and access-control conditions must directories, the database, lock, temporary files, value files, fixtures and spool files satisfy?

judgement.why: The topic repeats the prior judgement about ownership, permissions, file types and link requirements for private store objects.

precedent.topic: Ownership, file-type, permission, and link requirements for private store objects
quotes: The directory and everything in it are private to the kernel's user; the kernel refuses to start otherwise. Every file of the directory is opened without following symbolic links; a link found at start stops the start, and one found later makes that store call fail with nothing written.
precedent.why: The topic concerns the unchanged private-store and link-check passage, and the reopening change neither touched it nor made exact file types or hard-link counts newly consequential.

topics.topic: Runtime revalidation and response to later-unsafe storage objects
questions: If ownership or permissions become insecure after startup, does the next store call that encounters the object fail, does the kernel stop, or are permissions trusted until restart?
Are privacy properties checked on every open/create, and what happens when a later store call encounters an object that is no longer private?
If ownership, permissions, file type or link count becomes unsafe after start, must each affected store call refuse, or are those properties checked only at startup?

quotes:
The directory and everything in it are private to the kernel's user; the kernel refuses to start otherwise. Every
file of the directory is opened without following symbolic links; a link found at start stops the start, and one found later makes that store call
fail with nothing written.

open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on a lock file inside data_directory, opened without following links and held for the life of the process; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue and no file fixture record names, and create the database schema, the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

record_change: [PATH_OR_ARTIFACT_POLICY] Every file and directory under the data directory MUST be opened without following symbolic links; a symbolic link met by any call after start makes that call raise StoreInternalError with nothing written.
judgement.divergence: One implementation rechecks ownership and permission safety whenever an object is opened or created and rejects or stops after a runtime change; another trusts the startup check until restart. The owner notices whether requests continue against storage that has become accessible to another principal.
judgement.why: The texts define start-time privacy validation and runtime symbolic-link handling but do not decide runtime ownership or permission revalidation.

topics.topic: Startup operation ordering and failure precedence
questions: In what order are startup checks and cleanup performed, and which refusal is reported when several fail?

In what exact order are locking, layout validation, privacy and link checks, database opening, orphan cleanup, EffectAttempt recovery, run derivation, run advancement, and surface opening performed, and which failure is reported first?
In what order are A18 startup checks and cleanup performed, and which refusal is returned when several conditions fail?

judgement.why: The topic repeats the prior judgement about startup step order and first-failure precedence.

precedent.topic: Startup validation check order and failure precedence
quotes: run_start_sequence: [ORCHESTRATION] MUST call, in exactly this order and each exactly once: load_installation with config_path; check_installed_instances with the loaded Installation; open_store with that Installation's data_directory; probe_sandbox; recover_in_flight_attempts; recover_running_runs (A03 rule 8, A09 rule 1, A14 rule 5, A18).

run_start_sequence: [VALIDATION_ERROR] Every step is required: the first step that raises — InstallationRejectedError, RefusedError from the instance check, a store refusal, SandboxUnavailableError, StopRequiredError or any other exception — stops the sequence there and propagates unchanged to the caller with the step named in its reason; no later step runs and nothing is retried or skipped.

read_configuration: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise InstallationRejectedError naming the first failing check, in this order: config_path is not a regular file or is a symbolic link (checked without following links), is not owned by the process's effective user, or grants any permission to group or others; the bytes cannot be read or do not parse as one JSON object whose members are exactly the fields of Installation with their types; a service appears twice in service_instances or in service_credentials; a credential header name is not an HTTP field-name token (one or more of the token characters of RFC 9110: letters, digits and the symbols allowed there); a credential's secret_file is not an absolute path; the owner token or any agent token is shorter than the imported ACCESS_TOKEN_LENGTH_MIN constant; two tokens among the owner token and the agent tokens are equal; two agent tokens have the same name.
precedent.why: The later contracts fix both the order among startup modules and the order of checks inside configuration loading, with the first failure reported.

topics.topic: Acknowledgement point and required crash or power-loss durability
questions: At what point may a store call report success, and must every reported-success transaction survive a process crash and host power loss?
What crash model must the store survive, and what file, directory, and SQLite synchronization is required before a change is acknowledged?

judgement.why: The topic repeats the prior judgement about acknowledgement-time durability across process crashes and power loss.

precedent.topic: Crash-safe durable publication protocol for database records and files
quotes: record_change: [PATH_OR_ARTIFACT_POLICY] Durability order: every file a change names is published, fsynced and its directory fsynced before the change is committed, and the SQLite database runs with synchronous FULL, so after a power loss a committed record never names a missing or partial file; a file published by a change that then failed stays unnamed until the next start removes it (A18 rule 4).

put_value_bytes: [PATH_OR_ARTIFACT_POLICY] MUST store the bytes in the content-addressed area under their digest: when a file for that digest already exists it returns without writing; otherwise it writes a temporary file in the same area, flushes and fsyncs it, re-checks its digest and size, and renames it into place without overwriting, so a crash leaves either no file or the complete file and a completed file is never rewritten.
precedent.why: The later store notes define publication before commit, file and directory fsync, SQLite synchronous FULL, power-loss coverage and cleanup of unnamed residue.

topics.topic: Crash-consistent ordering of database records and referenced files

precedent.why: The later store notes define publication before commit, file and directory fsync, SQLite synchronous FULL, power-loss coverage and cleanup of unnamed residue.

precedent.topic: Exclusive-lock mechanism, ownership, failure classification, and crash release
quotes: open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on a lock file inside data_directory, opened without following links and held for the life of the process; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue and no file fixture record names, and create the database schema, the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

open_store: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise RefusedError whose reason names the failed check: data_directory does not exist (it is never created here), lock held by another process, directory not private (naming the first offending path), or symbolic link found (naming its path); it removes and creates nothing when a check fails.

serve_kernel: [VALIDATION_ERROR] When run_start_sequence raises, MUST write the failing step and the exception's reason to standard error, without any token, credential value, configuration content or stack trace, open no entrance and return a non-zero exit code; there is no partial start and no retry. Ending the process releases the store lock; nothing the steps already committed is rolled back, and the next start runs the whole sequence again from those records. Binding the listener at mcp_listen_address is the last start step and fails the same way, the step named open_entrance, when the address cannot be parsed as a host and port or the socket cannot be bound; a listener lost while serving ends the process with a non-zero exit code, without retry.
precedent.why: The later notes specify a non-blocking process-held lock file, its lifetime, lock-held refusal and automatic release when the process ends.

topics.topic: Meaning and process boundary of the one-process rule
questions: Does “one process” mean one long-lived kernel/store process while sandbox subprocesses are permitted, or literally no additional processes?
Does the one-process rule mean one long-lived coordinating kernel process while allowing transient sandbox child processes, or does it prohibit every additional OS process?

quotes: The kernel is one process.

Every function execution, in trial and in a run alike, runs in a fresh
isolated environment created by the sandbox: Linux `bubblewrap` with new user,
PID, IPC, UTS and network namespaces, no network interface, an environment
holding only `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` (rule 2), a read-only runtime, and one private exchange directory bounded by
`sandbox_scratch_bytes_max`.

An execution completes only after every process of the environment is reaped
and the exchange directory is removed.
judgement.why: The one-process rule describes the kernel while the sandbox rules expressly require transient isolated processes and their reaping.

topics.topic: Number and concurrency of SQLite connections
questions: May the store module open multiple SQLite connections sequentially or concurrently for reads, or must the process own exactly one connection for its lifetime?
May the store module open multiple SQLite connections, including concurrent read connections, or exactly one connection for the process?

quotes:
Reuses cabinet-flow decisions 30 and 32, narrowed by K-17: no store continuity, no
concurrent connections.
judgement.why: The reopened-state change did not touch the no-concurrent-connections passage or make the number of sequential connections newly consequential.

topics.topic: Symbolic-link prohibition scope, race resistance, and runtime response
questions: Which path components and object kinds are covered by the symbolic-link prohibition, and must traversal be component-by-component and race-resistant?
After a symbolic link is introduced during operation, is only the store call that encounters it refused, is every subsequent request refused, or must the kernel stop?
Which path components and object types are checked for links, and does a link introduced after start refuse only one call or stop/refuse the kernel globally?

quotes:
Every
file of the directory is opened without following symbolic links; a link found at start stops the start, and one found later makes that store call
fail with nothing written.

record_change: [PATH_OR_ARTIFACT_POLICY] Every file and directory under the data directory MUST be opened without following symbolic links; a symbolic link met by any call after start makes that call raise StoreInternalError with nothing written.

open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on a lock file inside data_directory, opened without following links and held for the life of the process; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue and no file fixture record names, and create the database schema, the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

The owner notices whether startup is refused and which filesystem location receives kernel data.
judgement.why: The later text settles runtime handling for links under the data directory but does not settle the data-directory path itself, its ancestors or race-resistant traversal of those components.

precedent.topic: Handling a conflicting existing file at a digest-derived path
quotes: put_value_bytes: [PATH_OR_ARTIFACT_POLICY] MUST store the bytes in the content-addressed area under their digest: when a file for that digest already exists it returns without writing; otherwise it writes a temporary file in the same area, flushes and fsyncs it, re-checks its digest and size, and renames it into place without overwriting, so a crash leaves either no file or the complete file and a completed file is never rewritten.
precedent.why: The later store contract explicitly returns without inspecting or replacing an existing digest-path file.
